output.situation: The user works shifts that change every week and keeps abandoning exercise, and they want a routine that does not rely on a fixed schedule. They have not said how far ahead they learn their shifts, what kind of exercise they tried, or what the stopping point usually looked like. The decisive unknown is how early the schedule is known, plus whether past quits followed one missed day or weeks of fatigue. The three minds below are fictional.

minds.title: The Time Realist
minds.concern: Plans built on control of time fail, so the routine should expect a messy week and still work.
minds.author: Oliver Burkeman

minds.title: The Cue Designer
minds.concern: Behavior follows obvious cues and small steps, so the design matters more than motivation.
minds.author: James Clear

minds.title: The Habit Drillmaster
minds.concern: A new habit needs a strong start and few exceptions, or early lapses undo the work.
minds.author: William James

debate.speaker: The Time Realist
debate.text: Start with the odd fit. Shifts change weekly, yet the usual plan assumes the same week every time. Benjamin Franklin admitted a fixed daily order was the virtue he mastered least, because running a print shop meant other people set his hours. My reading: the plan keeps breaking, and giving up is just what that breakage gets called.
debate.author: Oliver Burkeman
debate.basis: Basis: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks (on the limits of controlling time); source not verified, no link provided. The Franklin example is a general reference, not attributed to Burkeman.

debate.speaker: The Cue Designer
debate.text: Taking only the why. Behavior needs a trigger it can see, and a clock time that moves each week is a trigger that keeps vanishing. Nothing dramatic happens; the workout simply never gets cued, and a habit with no cue gets filed under good intentions. That is a design flaw, not a character one.
debate.author: James Clear
debate.basis: Basis: James Clear, Atomic Habits (on cues and making habits obvious); source not verified, no link provided.

debate.speaker: The Habit Drillmaster
debate.text: Only the how. Choose one thing that never moves and keep it without exception until it takes root. William James argued a new habit needs a strong start, and that each early lapse undoes many repetitions. Flexible plans sound wise and let every tired day talk its way out.
debate.author: William James
debate.basis: Basis: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), chapter on habit; paraphrased, source not verified, no link provided.

debate.speaker: The Time Realist
debate.text: The story told about Jerry Seinfeld and his calendar chain is your best case, and it works because writing a joke takes minutes. A flat no-exceptions rule on a full workout, after a night shift that flipped the sleep, costs rest. If protecting sleep is the real worry, the rule should shrink to a walk.
debate.author: Oliver Burkeman
debate.basis: Basis: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks (on accepting limits and tradeoffs); source not verified, no link provided. The extension to sleep and shift work is the mind own thinking.

debate.speaker: The Habit Drillmaster
debate.text: That lands. I was treating exercise as one size, and a ninety-minute session after a flipped night is not the same thing as ten minutes. I am narrowing my rule: the no-exception part applies only to a small floor, and the full workout floats. Sleep is what moved me.
debate.author: William James
debate.basis: Basis: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), chapter on habit; paraphrased, source not verified, no link provided. The narrowing to a small floor is the mind own revision.

debate.speaker: The Cue Designer
debate.text: A floor still needs something to hang from. Shifts change, but people still wake, eat, and leave for work, so the ten minutes can follow one of those, like right after locking the front door. The British cycling team under Dave Brailsford chased small gains over big overhauls. Small and attached beats small and floating.
debate.author: James Clear
debate.basis: Basis: James Clear, Atomic Habits (habit stacking and small gains); source not verified, no link provided.

debate.speaker: The Time Realist
debate.text: One possibility to test. They wrote that they keep giving up, which might mean each lapse reads to them as proof about themselves, not about the plan. If that is happening, the design has to make a missed day harmless. If instead quitting follows injury or exhaustion, this reading fails.
debate.author: Oliver Burkeman
debate.basis: Basis: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks (on perfectionism and limits); source not verified, no link provided.

debate.speaker: The Habit Drillmaster
debate.text: I reject that reading, because nothing they wrote mentions blaming themselves; people drop oversized plans with no verdict on their character. My rival: the opening plan was too big, so the first bad week ended it. What follows is that the first month of the floor deserves the strictest guarding.
debate.author: William James
debate.basis: Basis: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), chapter on habit; paraphrased, source not verified, no link provided.

debate.speaker: The Cue Designer
debate.text: Another possibility. They asked for a routine that does not depend on the same schedule, which might mean they want it automatic, with no daily deciding. But they also work shifts that move, which means following them. Both cannot be fully had: a cue-attached floor serves the automatic wish, and a weekly look at the roster serves the flexible one.
debate.author: James Clear
debate.basis: Basis: James Clear, Atomic Habits (on cues, environment, and habit stacking); source not verified, no link provided.

debate.speaker: The Time Realist
debate.text: I offer a rival reading: not automatic, but forgiving, meaning they can miss a week and restart without ceremony. If so, a short Sunday planning slot is not a cost to hide, it is the routine itself. Cues help the floor; the bigger session needs a person choosing a slot.
debate.author: Oliver Burkeman
debate.basis: Basis: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks (on deliberate choices among limited hours); source not verified, no link provided.

debate.speaker: The Habit Drillmaster
debate.text: Here is the missing fact: how early they learn the next shifts. If the roster is posted a week ahead, I would write the floor into actual slots, because a decided slot beats a hoped-for one. If shifts change the same day, slots collapse and I would switch to the cue-attached floor.
debate.author: William James
debate.basis: Basis: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), chapter on habit; paraphrased, source not verified, no link provided. The conditional on roster timing is the mind own thinking.

debate.speaker: The Cue Designer
debate.text: Our open fight is whether the floor is a hard rule or a cue with room to miss. I favor missing once but never twice; the other view calls that a leak. A fact not given decides it: if past stops began with one skipped day snowballing, strictness wins; if they came from weeks of piling fatigue, permission wins.
debate.author: James Clear
debate.basis: Basis: James Clear, Atomic Habits (never miss twice); source not verified, no link provided.

output.clearer: The main insight is that a clock-based plan is a poor fit for a changing roster, so the routine may need a small floor attached to events that still happen (waking, leaving work) with a larger session placed week by week. Still disputed: whether that floor should be a strict no-exception rule or a cue that allows one miss, and whether the wish is for automatic or merely forgiving. A possible self-reflection: when past attempts ended, did they end after a single skipped day, after a long run of tiredness, or because the plan was too big to begin with? Sources were not verified in this run, and the attributions are paraphrased.
output.dependsOn:
If the roster is known about a week ahead: a short weekly planning slot that places the floor and one larger session becomes more reasonable, because decided slots are easier to keep than hoped-for ones.
If shifts change on the same day: a small floor tied to an event that always happens (leaving work, waking up) becomes more reasonable, because no slot survives the changes.
If past stops began with one skipped day turning into weeks: a stricter floor with few exceptions becomes more reasonable, because early lapses are what did the damage.
If past stops came from accumulating fatigue or poor sleep: a lighter floor, such as a walk, with permission to miss once becomes more reasonable, because rest is what is being protected.
If these facts stay unknown: try a ten-minute floor for two or three weeks of rosters, note when it breaks, and let that record show which case applies.
